If poverty and unemployment rise alongside output, the gains are accruing to a narrow section and the standard of living of the mass of people has not improved, so the higher figure does not signify development. Sectoral imbalances and a widening trade gap may be problems in themselves, but neither directly contradicts a claim about the level of development in the way rising poverty does.

answers.value: Statements 2 and 4 — raising knowledge, skills and capacities of people, which is accumulation of intangible wealth

Because the resulting asset is embodied in human beings and cannot be separated from them, it is intangible wealth, so statement 4 also holds. Statements 1 and 3 describe physical capital formation — accumulating capital goods and tangible wealth — which is a different process from the formation of human capital.

answers.value: A high capital-output ratio

When that ratio is high, each rupee of investment yields comparatively little extra output, so even an economy that saves and invests heavily records only a modest rise in production — the Harrod-Domar relation, in which the growth rate equals the saving rate divided by the capital-output ratio, makes this explicit. Weak administration, illiteracy and population density can all impair growth, but the ratio is the direct link between capital formation and output that the question asks about.

Both statements therefore describe real post-rebellion measures.

answers.value: All three - the Charter Act of 1813, the General Committee of Public Instruction of 1823 and the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy

The Charter Act of 1813 first made the Company responsible for education and set aside one lakh rupees a year for it, creating the fund that had to be spent. The General Committee of Public Instruction, constituted in 1823, was the body created to spend that money and to decide the shape of instruction. Within that Committee the Orientalists, who wanted classical Indian learning supported, and the Anglicists, who wanted English and European science, deadlocked, and the controversy was resolved by Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's resolution of 1835 in favour of English education. Each step therefore led to the introduction of English education.
